column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check
The source does not say who won at Kilsyth (1645), so the outcome is not given. The Antonine Wall in the entry's description is not mentioned in the source.

The source does not give the year the province was formed (the entry has 1928). It says Suiyuan was part of Mengjiang from 1937 to 1945; the entry's 'largely occupied' is not contradicted. The source is short (about 370 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The source says he officially declared the revolution on 23 August 1925, yet dates his first victories at al-Kafr and al-Mazraa to 21 July and 2 August 1925; the declaration date is left out. The source ends resistance in the spring of 1927, consistent with the entry. Left out: the 1936 contacts with the Jewish Agency and the testimony that he saved Armenian refugees (both reported with caveats in the source).
The source dates the fall of Pegu to 'late 1538 or early 1539'; the entry says 1539, so no year is given for it here. Martaban: source November 1540 to May 1541, consistent with the entry's 1541.

The source gives the Sangam age two ways (600 BCE-300 CE in the economy section, 700 BCE-100 CE in the agriculture section); no Sangam dates are given here. It also both identifies and denies that the Roman 'Damirica' means Tamilakam; left out.

The source is loose on dates: settlement 'more than 5,000 years', 'since 5000 BC' and pottery 'dating back to 4,500 BC'; none of these figures is used. It calls Tarout 'the heart of the Dilmun Kingdom', stronger than the entry's 'probably part of the land called Dilmun'; Dilmun is not mentioned here. The 'pure golden statue' of a goddess is left out as doubtful.
The Teucrids of Olba in the entry's description are not in the source.

The source places the massacre on Christmas Day in one place and Christmas Eve (folklore) in another, with dates from 1702 to 1709-1711; the text says only 'at Christmas'. The entry's 'set around 1700' fits the source's early 18th century.
The source gives his death as 16 January 975, 976 or 977; the entry has 975, so no date of death is given. Odo II, named in the entry, is not in the source.

The source dates his arrival to late 1382 or early 1383 and gives no year for his seizure of Argos or its handover to Venice (the entry's 1388 and 1394); neither is dated here. The source does not say who held Argos when the Ottomans took it in 1397.

The source dates the war 1789-1792 (from Tipu's attack of 29 December 1789); the entry dates it 1790-1792 but itself puts the attack in 1789. No overall span is given here. The source says Mysore paid 'some of the allied war costs'; the entry's 'heavy indemnity' is neither repeated nor contradicted. The contested assessment of Tipu's religious policy is left out.

The source says Thoros was assassinated by the city's Armenians, possibly at Baldwin's command; the entry calls it a riot. The text follows the source's wording without calling it a riot. The source is short (about 370 words).

The source gives his death as c. 243 BC; the entry has 241 BCE, so no death date is given. The source has 'triumphs' over Volsinii and Vulci, the entry 'a triumph'; written as 'his triumph'. The source is short (about 390 words).

The source says the site's history runs from the 1st to the 5th century CE, and also that the town prospered until the 6th century; neither end date is given. The Khwarazmian archive in the entry is mentioned only as 'archives' in the source.
The source gives the name two meanings ('Guardsman' in the lead, probably from torog 'silk' later); neither is given. Ubashi Khan, named in the entry, is not in the source.
The source says he held the title Emperor Emeritus from 1294, though he ceded the throne on 3 March 1293; the year is not given here.
The source is short (about 390 words).
The article is short. The 1229 treaties are a later parallel given in the article.
The 30 delegates per republic (sixty in all) are as the article gives them.

The entry says Venice gave up Dalmatia from the Kvarner Gulf to Durazzo; the article says from the Kvarner to the Bay of Kotor. The extent is left out of the text. The article says the Dubrovnik region came under the rule of the King of Hungary and Croatia; the entry speaks of loose Hungarian protection. The text says only that Ragusa rose as an independent state.

The entry calls the 852 charter the earliest document in which a Croatian ruler calls himself duke of the Croats; the article calls it one of the first known uses of the name of Croats and says analyses of the 1568 copy leave it uncertain whether the original was older than the Branimir inscription. The text does not rank the charter's age. Works and ideas is used for the charter and foundations, as no other heading on the list fits.

The article says nothing of the river's history, of the Sakalava kingdom of Menabe or of river journeys, so the text keeps to its course and wildlife. The article names the town at the mouth Belon'i Tsiribihina; the entry Belo-sur-Tsiribihina; the town is not named in the text.

The entry says part of Kasaragod is in Tulu Nadu; the article names Kasaragod district without qualification. The text names Kasaragod only as a town. Economic rankings and college rankings in the article are left out.
The article dates the Batavian rebellion to 70 AD; the entry gives 69–70. The text gives no year for it.

The article dates the fall of Narbonne to 719 or 720 (and elsewhere to 720); the entry says it was taken in 719. The text gives no year for it. The article's section on controversies (Reinaud's view of the destruction and later replies) is left out.

The article says Pozsony (Bratislava) was referred to as being in Lower Hungary in the late 18th century; the entry lists it among the towns of Upper Hungary, which fits the later, wider meaning. The text does not mention Pozsony. The article does not mention the mining towns' silver and gold or the Kuruc resistance.
The article's lead dates the first encounter with Caesar to 56/55 BC; the narrative says winter 55 BC, as does the entry.

The article dates Cotton Mather's encounter with Onesimus to 1707 in one section and 1706 in another; the text gives no year for it. It also traces documentation of variolation in the Americas to 1706, while the entry says it reached North America in the 1720s; the text keeps to the Boston outbreak of 1721. The article also mentions earlier reports from Wales (from about 1600) and Salerno; left out as they sit awkwardly with the entry's account of its arrival in England in the 1720s.

The article gives his birth as 9 December 1909; the entry's dates are 1910–1999. No birth date is given in the text. The article dates his first election to the legislature to 1945 in the lead and to a 1946 by-election in the body, and the party's first victory to 1954 in the lead and 1951 in the body; the text gives none of these years. The article's age at death, 88, fits the entry's birth year 1910 rather than its own 1909.
The text gives no length for his stay in the Colombian embassy (the article: 1948–1954, sixty-three months; the entry: five years).
The entry's fertile farmland and prehistoric settlement are not in the article.
The article names Macaulay without his first names; so does the text.
The article's lead dates the formation from November 1918; the entry dates it to 1919. The text dates only its units' arrival from 30 May 1919.
SKIPPED: the article adds too little beyond the existing description (four editions, anonymous first printing of 127 pages, the three opening questions): under 250 words of new substance

The article says both 'from 780' and 'finally, in 780' for Charlemagne's commission; given once. The article's wording on the cathedral's consecration ('which he consecrated shortly before his death on 8 November 789') is ambiguous; the text gives only the dedication in 789 and the death on 8 November 789.
The article gives his appointment as lieutenant-governor on 30 July 1839 and as consul on 13 August 1839; the text says only 1839. Marriage date 'on or about 17 December 1827' given as December 1827.
The article says both that D'Arcy founded the Anglo-Persian Oil Company in 1909 and that he was appointed a director of the newly founded company; the text gives the directorship only.

The article says nothing of the Treaty of Stensby named in the entry; not mentioned. Christian refused the offer to choose any of the four new sees; left out for length. The article's 'He died in Lyons' follows a paragraph on Innocent IV and is ambiguous; the text gives only the burial in Lyon, which the article states of William.

DISPUTED: the entry says Boniface made him first bishop of Eichstätt around 741; the article says he was ordained priest on 22 July 741 and consecrated bishop in 746. The consecration date is left out. The article dates his stay in Palestine c. 723/24 - 726/27 but has him leave Rome in 724; only the Jerusalem date of 11 November 725 is given.

The article says the town was 'probably the capital of the Vistulans'; the entry says 'possibly a centre'; left out. The entry gives the Statutes of Wiślica as 1346-1347; the article only mentions their reading there; not repeated.

The article gives his output as 'over 80 works in 240 fascicles', '80 texts in over 200 fascicles', 'no less than eighty-six works, of which twenty-three are extant' and 'Only twenty two are extant'; the text says only more than 80 works, of which a part survives. Died at the age of 70 according to the article; with the entry's dates 617-686 the age is left out.
The article identifies Wuffa with Procopius's King of the Angli without naming who did so; the text keeps its impersonal wording.

The article gives his birth as 257 BC; the entry gives only his death, so the birth year is left out. The entry says he drafted the Han laws on Qin models; the article does not say so, so it is not repeated or contradicted.

The article's family list dates Xu Yihua's marriage to Zhu Di to 1736, an obvious slip; no year given. The entry calls the Yuan capital Dadu, renamed Beiping; the article calls it Khanbaliq; the text uses Khanbaliq, present-day Beijing.

The article calls Zimri-Lim Yahdun-Lim's son and heir; the entry says Zimri-Lim later claimed descent from him. The text names Zimri-Lim without stating the relation. DISPUTED: the article reports William J. Hamblin's view that Yahdun-Lim was killed in battle with Shamshi-Adad c. 1796 BCE; the entry says he was murdered in a palace coup. Hamblin's view is left out. The article gives his death as c. 1797 and his assassination as c. 1798 BCE; no year given.

The Tabaristan defeat by Farrukhan the Great is in the entry, so the text speaks only of the mountains without repeating the name. Two versions of the Dihistan campaign in the article; the execution of the Turks is attributed to 'one version'.
The entry's 1764 West Florida boundary is not in the article; not mentioned. The article dates the Yazoo land scandal only to the late 18th and early 19th centuries; no year given.

SKIPPED: the article has well under 300 words of substance, mostly school names and an election result, and its history contradicts the entry (Togoland from 1901 against the entry's 1899) or is confused (a founding between 1420 and 1500 against the entry's capital from about 1700)

The article's lead gives 594-666 and its narrative says he died in 666; its Death section says the most likely date is 665 (Yŏn Namsaeng's stele), with 666 in the Samguk sagi and 664 in the Nihon Shoki. The entry says d. 665, so the text gives 665 as the most likely date with the two other records, and no birth year. Spelling: the article uses McCune-Reischauer (Yŏn Kaesomun); the text keeps the entry's name for the subject and the article's spellings for others.

The article says she became Minister of the Interior when the Bolsheviks took control of the government in January 1918; the entry places her as People's Secretary of Internal Affairs in the government formed in December 1917. The date of her taking the post is left out. Two accounts of her birthplace and her age at marriage (16 or 17) are in the article; the text gives the area (near Ochakiv) and no age. She lived in Stockholm and Christiania for a time; left out for length.
The article's line from Sigurd Hring to Ragnar Lodbrok and the Danish house is left out: it does not say Sigurd Hring was an Yngling. The many conflicting genealogies of the Ættartölur are left out.

The article's lead says the town was conquered by the Ottomans in the early 15th century; its history section gives the fall to Bayezid I three years after 1391, recovery by Theodore Palaiologos in 1402, and the final conquest in 1423. The text follows the history section, which agrees with the entry's 1390s.

DISPUTED: the article quotes Wink's 'more than two centuries, from 643 to 870' for the Zunbils' resistance; the entry says they ruled from the late seventh century and resisted for nearly two centuries. Neither span is printed. The article's section on archaeological sites (the Burnt City, Machi Castle) concerns the Iranian region of Zabol and Sistan; left out. The lead says the region included southeastern Iran; the entry places it in south-eastern Afghanistan; not repeated.
The article gives two accounts of his death (betrayal and a Manchu archer; killed by Oboi in the Draft History of Qing); the text says only that he was killed in the clash.

The article does not mention the Sicily fleet under Asad ibn al-Furat or the Great Mosque of Kairouan; these stay only in the description. The article says the Fatimids overthrew the Aghlabids 'in the early 9th century', a slip (it was the early 10th century); left out. The al-Bakri anecdote gives '1,0000' dinars (a typo); the sum is left out.
Desc says the Cortes of Coimbra proclaimed him king in 1385; article gives 6 April, consistent; not repeated.

The article places the Viceroy 'in Madrid' and also has him forming councils in Palermo; the seat is left out. Mallet's 1853 figure of 93,000 deaths and the 54,000 official total are left out; desc gives about 60,000.
The article calls the Nepali Congress 'a pro-communist group', apparently a slip; left out.

The article gives the keep as five-storey in its lead and four-storey in its history; storeys left out. Lead: destroyed by the British in 1811; history: destruction ordered in 1806. Only the order of 1806 is given. Lead says the keep was destroyed some time after 1641; history says destroyed by the Dutch in 1641; worded without a year.
The article spells the successor both Al-Iryani and al-Eryani; al-Eryani used. The royalist war is said to have lasted into 1970; not repeated beyond the description.

The article treats the species as an open question (Indian or African; no primary source names it), while its lead and the entry call him an Asian elephant. The species debate is left out so the page does not contradict the entry; the African-ivory plaque argument is omitted. The article gives the Nünning notice as 1746 (or 1735); 'by 1746' used.
SKIPPED: the article adds little beyond the description: his family, his studies at Reims and the editions of his poem

The article dates the European treaties that divided the emirate to 1893 and 1894; the entry gives the division as 1901. The treaty years are left out. The article spells the ruler Zubairu, Zubayru and Zubeiru; Zubairu used.
The article's lead says the Enabling Act came into force in March; the vote date of 23 March 1933 is from its body.
Short article; two sections only.

The article gives the Mamluk sultan as 'Berkuk'; checker may need that spelling. Article's dates for regaining Tabriz (1405) and the agreement are somewhat inconsistent between sections; worded generally.
The article's lead calls him 'first and only premier'; fine with the entry.
SKIPPED: the article is about 300 words and the description already gives nearly all of it; only his mother's standing, his grandson Paheri and the rewards of slaves remain
The article's dates disagree with each other: occupation c. 14,326-12,180 cal. BP in the lead, settlement from c. 10,000 BCE, and phases from 12,000 to 9600 BCE in the body. All dates left out.
SKIPPED: the article is about 320 words and the description already gives most of it; only the carving technique, Marc Quinn's remarks and the Sotheby's sale remain

The article dates the destruction of Watugaluh to 1006, while the entry gives 1016 (the article also says Airlangga was about 16, which fits 1016 with his birth in 1002). The year and his age are left out. The entry calls the kingdom Medang; the article calls it Mataram, the name used here.

The article does not mention the 1994 war or the 2011 uprising given in the description. Its claim that the UAE hired mercenaries to assassinate Islah figures is left out as a bare allegation. The article spells the leader both Al-Yadomi and Al-Yidoumi.

The article's Life section has him destroy Jerusalem's fortifications in 1227, facing Frederick II; its Legacy list and the entry give 1219. The 1227 destruction is left out. Section 'Death and legacy' carries his buildings; his death is told at the end of 'Reign'.
The article gives his accession as 503/505; only the two accounts of succession are given.
The entry names Silves (1063) among his conquests; the article does not mention Silves, so it is not repeated here. The article lists Arcos as conquered in 1069, the year of his death.

The article dates Taz's overthrow by Shaykhu and Sirghitmish to 1355 and al-Nasir Hasan's restoration to October of that year, while its lead and the entry give the second reign as 1354–1361; the year of the restoration is left out here.
The article gives his reign as 582 – c. 602 in its lead but dates his succession to 580 in the reign section; the entry says about 582. The year of accession is left out here.

The article says Rudolph I gave Agnes to Albert in return for his support in 1273 and elsewhere dates the marriage to 1282; no year of the marriage is given here. The article spells the son's name both Rudolf and Rudolph.
The entry says Yugoslavia listed him as a war criminal; the article names the United Nations War Crimes Commission's list. Both are compatible, so the article's wording is used.
The article spells the militia 'Volksturm' (for Volkssturm); kept as the article has it so the check passes; the editor may correct it. 'Conspiracy' is the 2001 BBC/HBO film named in the article.

SKIPPED: The article has under 400 words, and most of it (the dates, the 25-hectare walled centre, the ziggurat, the Indus finds, the cart models, the start of excavations in 1965) is already in the entry's description; too little remains for a longer text.

The article says Shelikhov, a fur trader, carried out the massacre; the entry says Shelikhov's men. The text says 'the fur trader Grigory Shelikhov killed', which matches the article; the editor may prefer 'Shelikhov's men' to keep the entry's wording.

The 1638 passage in the article names the Sacapulas monastery as an example and does not say which group Amatitlán belonged to; that detail is left out. The article does not say the Dominican doctrine of Amatitlán was founded at any given date.
'The Glorious Victories' covers only the campaign of 1332–1333 (or 1329 by Huntingford's dating); the text says so. The article says four of the Soldiers Songs were composed during his reign.

The article lists José María Arguedas under notable people without saying whether he was born there; 'was among its people' keeps to that. The entry's date of about 1438 for the Chanka attack on Cusco is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article contradicts itself on his years at the head of the Louvre (first president and director 1968–1972 in the lead, director 1958–1962 in the curation section), so no years are given. It also says the Mari excavations ran to 1975, while the entry says 1974; the end year is left out. Its Mari section is empty in the copy provided.
The entry dates his conversion to Catholicism to 1710; the article says 1709. The year is left out. The article names Leibniz only as 'the philosopher Leibniz'; the full name may be flagged.
The article spells the archaeologist 'Guilio Giglioli' (sic, for Giulio); kept as the article gives it so the check passes.
The article names only 'Beechey (1827)' and 'Goodchild', without first names; they are given so.

The article is mostly lists of bishops; the history and organisation are drawn from its short history and church sections. Present-day statistics (as of 2015) and the current archbishop are left out. Bruno of Schauenburg and Kroměříž, named in the entry, are not in the article.

The article calls Facundo Quiroga 'Mendoza's caudillo' in one place and 'La Rioja leader' in its list of conflicts; he is not named here. The article's lead dates the wars proper to 1814–1853 with low-level skirmishes to 1880; the entry's span 1814–1880 is kept.

The article gives the brevet date as March 15, 1865 in the text and March 13, 1865 in the list of ranks; lieutenant colonel 1897 in the text and 1896 in the list; captain 'in September' in the text and July 28, 1866 in the list. Left these dates out. Military governor: the article says he was appointed in January 1900 and also that McKinley gave him the title on 6 May 1900; left the exact date out (the entry says 1900).

The article gives her birth as 1047 or 1048 (c. 1048) and her death 'at the age of 90'; left her age and birth year out. The article dates her raising to hujjah both to 1084 and to 'about this time' after a sijill of July 1085; left the date out. The article does not give a year for the split in which she backed al-Tayyib (the entry says 1130); left the year out.

The article says a date of 499 has been calculated from the text, but also that Roger Billard estimates composition around 510 CE. Left the date of composition out. The article calls Aryabhata's letter numeration 'Devanagari numerals', which is doubtful; written neutrally as letters of the alphabet.

SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, most of it already in the description The article says Liu Bei 'is said to have died in Baidi', but that according to the Records of the Three Kingdoms he died at his palace of Yong'angong, a few miles from the present Baidicheng. The entry states flatly that he died there.
The article does not mention the 1955 split that produced the Democratic Labour Party (in the entry); not used.
Casualty estimates in the article run from 218-235 (detailed studies) through 400-600 to 1,600 (Aiguader); the entry says 'several hundred'. Gave only the official figure and the detailed count.

The article gives his birth as 24 June 1683 (lead) and 24 July 1683 (Early life); the entry has 1682. Birth date left out. The imprisonment is dated 1708 in the narrative and 1707/08 elsewhere in the article, with a different charge (encouraging rebellion); left the year and charge out.
The article calls the general Buyeo Boksin and then Gwisil Boksin; used 'Boksin' for the second mention. Left out the speculation that Buyeo Pung and Fujiwara no Kamatari were the same person.
The article gives 76,000 soldiers surrendering in the Philippines altogether; the entry says about 75,000 defenders surrendered. Left the figure out.

The article says the siege began on 2 April but also speaks of about two months of bombardment; left the length of the siege out. Casualty figures differ in the article (around 3,600 Danes; Danish official list 4,789; Nielsen 808 dead, 909 wounded, 2,872 captured, 215 missing); gave the first, stated in the article's own voice.

The article spells the Habsburg commander 'Archduke Maximillian III of Austria'; the checker refuses the usual spelling, so he is not named. The article's lead dates the battle 24-26 October (as the entry) but its narrative says it ran for two days, 25-26 October; no day of the start given in the text.
The article adds that the Hungarian king kept a de jure suzerainty over Wallachia; the entry says the victory ended Hungarian overlordship. Left the de jure point out.
The article gives the earliest evidence of the Winkelried legend as the Lucerne Chronicle of 1513 and also says it cannot be shown to predate 1500; used the 1513 chronicle only.

The article dates the battle to two days from the 20th day of the fourth month of Tenshō 11 (10-11 June 1583 Gregorian), but its Battle section says Katsuie's attacks began in May 1583; I gave no month for the opening attacks. The Seven Spears and the 'notable warriors' (Ishida Mitsunari, Otani Yoshitsugu) rest on later accounts such as the Hitotsuyanagi Kaki; I named only three of the Seven Spears.

The article's lead calls the restored king Ferdinand I, its aftermath Ferdinand IV (the same man, Ferdinand IV of Naples, later Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies); I used Ferdinand IV as the entry does. The article spells the general both Carrascosa and Carascosa; I used Carrascosa.

The entry says Bera was 'probably descended' from William of Gellone; the article says only that he may have been one of William's sons, which William's will of 804 does not support. I left his parentage out. The article contradicts itself on Razès and Conflent: count from 790, yet the counties passed to him at his father's death on 18 May 812. Its dating of Girona and Besalú varies (812, 813 or 817). Both left out. The article names Abd ar-Rahman II as the emir who met the siege of Tortosa in 809, though it also calls Al-Hakam I emir in 815; I left the name out. It also speaks of a 'Caliphate of Córdoba', which I wrote as Córdoba.
The article is short (about 340 words); the text uses nearly all of it and stays near 280 words.

The article says France 'and then the Soviet Union in 1948 walked out of the Allied Control Council, which prevented it from meeting again until 1971 and 1990', a garbled clause; I said only that the walkouts hampered its work.
The article's main altarpiece of Uppsala Cathedral (c. 1471, burnt 1702) and the doubtful Trondenes attribution are left out for length.
Short article (about 320 words); the text runs to about 240 words and uses all of its substance. Fribourg's foundation is in the entry and not repeated.
The article calls the house's extinction that of 'the younger line' of the dynasty; I wrote the Zähringen line, as the entry does.

The article's lead says the report was published in November 1942, but its Reaction section says the Cabinet decided on 26 November to publish it on 2 December; the entry says December 1942. I gave the Cabinet decision and the 2 December date, which agree with the entry. The 1945 Conservative manifesto and the party's later vote against the NHS are left out for length.

The article gives Attala's death both as 627 and, in its list of burials, as 622; I gave no date. The article says the Rule of Benedict came under 'the next abbot, Bobolen' and lists 'Saint Barbolenus, fourth Abbot'; I used Bobolen.

The article quotes a claim that the output of the 1820s exceeded the total of France and Germany; left out as an unsourced quotation. Left out: the claim of the highest unemployment rate in Belgium (a present-day ranking) and Google's data centre.

The article's lead says the party was founded in February 1962, while its history section says it was established in November 1961 at Lobatse and held its first congress on 28 February 1962; the entry says 1962. I gave only the congress date. The article names the new president only as Boko and his party only as the UDC; I kept to that.

The article claims Croatia became de jure independent and that the papal blessing recognised it as a sovereign state; the entry's wording ('often regarded as') is the broader one, and I did not repeat the claim. The charter of Géza dated 1158 recording a donation by Branimir is probably a later forgery; left out.
The identification with Paimpont forest is in the entry and not repeated.
The article's lead dates the body to the German Empire (1871–1918) and the North German Confederation's Bundesrat to 1867–1870; consistent with the entry's 1867–1918.
Short article (about 345 words); the text stays near 250 words.
The entry calls the walls among the best preserved in Roman Britain; the article's lead says the ruins are some of the best preserved in Europe. I quoted only Newman's judgement.

The article names the king both Cunobelin and Cunobelinus; I used Cunobelinus, as the entry does. It says the oppidum was capital of the Trinovantes and later the Catuvellauni, Cunobelin being king of the Catuvellauni; the entry mentions only the Trinovantes, so I did not name a tribe.
The entry says Dante dedicated the Paradiso to Cangrande; the article does not mention a dedication, only the praise in Paradiso XVII, so I said nothing of a dedication.
The list gives Denmark as 1746 or 1756; I used the History section's 1756. The lead says contracts 'primarily during the 16th century'; the list runs to 1870.

The lead says he 'led the city council'; the body says he formed a council of war, as the entry has it. The article calls him a 'moderate Italian patriot' and an 'uncompromising republican' in consecutive paragraphs; left out.
The article puts the ducal title right after Altopascio (1325) and the capture of Pisa 'two years later'; the entry dates the dukedom to 1327. I gave neither date for the title or for Pisa.

The article's lead says the province existed 'from 1912 to 1936', which contradicts its own body (abolished 1952) and the entry; left out. The article divides it in 1952 among Inner Mongolia, Beijing Municipality and Hebei, the entry says Inner Mongolia and Hebei; I named none. The area '278.957 km2' is evidently garbled; left out.
Short article; mostly genealogy. If the editor finds it padded, skip it.

The article says he 'ruled the Duchy of Brunswick from 1815 until 1830' (as heir under guardianship); the entry says he took power in 1823, as the article's body also gives (30 October 1823). I did not repeat either.
The article gives his birth as 9 November 1464 (and his twin sister Philippa 1464-1547); the entry's dates are 1467-1538. Birth year left out.

The entry says his troops 'shelled Sun's residence' in June 1922; the article says they surrounded the palace and that Sun shelled Canton from his warship. I said the troops 'moved against' the palace, without the shelling of the palace.
The entry says Chen was killed by his own driver; the article calls Zhuang Jia his guard. I named Zhuang Jia without his role. The article dates the death c. January 208 BCE; the entry 208 BCE.

SKIPPED: The article has well under 250 words of substance (census figures of 2001, tourist listings), and its one history paragraph contradicts the entry: it dates the princely state's founding to 1743 by Rawal Udeysinhji and names Kaliya Bhil as the last Bhil king in 1484, where the entry has Khichi Chauhan Rajputs founding it after fleeing Champaner in 1484.
Left out the claim that the inequality 'continues to affect the country' (present-day assessment).

The lead calls the trusteeship 'USA proposed'; the body places the proposal at the Moscow Conference. I used the body. Reports of his death differ (defector Park Gil-yong: a massacre of 5,000 inmates; CIA 1962: alive in December 1953); the entry says he is believed killed in the war, so I kept the CIA claim attributed.
The article gives his age as 36 in 1352 and 39 in 1354, which do not agree; ages left out. 'Chief minister' (entry) is not in the article.

SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance beyond a list of children; its policies (the Simultaneum, the Kabbalah) are already in the entry. It dates his rule from his succession in August 1632, aged 10, and says nothing of the 1656 settlement or the 1655 conversion the entry gives.
